2915.t: From Proto-Hellenic *lúkos, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos (“wolf”) with metathesis. Cognates include Sanskrit वृक (vṛ́ka), Latin lupus (also showing metathesis), Old English wulf (English wolf) and Russian волк (volk).

2910.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kórwā, whence also Mycenaean Greek 𐀒𐀷 (ko-wa). In this word, α (ā) shifted to η (ē) in Attic (see Attic–Ionic vowel shift on Wikipedia) because of the preceding ϝ (w).

2974.t: Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-tís. By surface analysis, φύω (phŭ́ō, “grow”) + -σις (-sĭs).

2990.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ayerīston, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyeri-h₁d-to-. First part in ἦρι (êri, “early”), second is zero-grade of ἔδω (édō, “to eat”), thus “early meal”.

2971.t: From Proto-Indo-European *téḱ-sneh₂, from *tetḱ- (“to create, produce”). Cognate with τίκτω (tíktō), τέκτων (téktōn), Sanskrit तक्षति (takṣati), Avestan 𐬙𐬀𐬱𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (tašaⁱti), Latin texō, tēla, tignum, Proto-Germanic *þahsuz.

2924.t: From Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂- (“to flow, to swim”). Cognate with Ναϊάς (Naïás), Νηρεύς (Nēreús), Latin nō, Sanskrit स्नौति (snauti, “to flow; drip”).

2906.t: According to Beekes, the word is Pre-Greek — which Beekes claims is the case for all Greek words with the -αλλο- suffix.

2945.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pléwō, from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to sail, flow”). In the present and imperfect, the semivowel *ϝ is lost between vowels, but before a consonant is kept as υ, the second element of a diphthong.

2970.t: For earlier τάμνω (támnō), with ε (e) from aorist ἔτεμον (étemon), from Proto-Indo-European *tm̥-né-h₁-ti, *tm̥-n-h₁-énti, nasal-infixed present (the present tense system includes a N progressive aspect marker) from *temh₁- (“to cut”).

2989.t: From Proto-Hellenic *armód͏̌d͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join, fit, fix together”).

2904.t: From Proto-Indo-European *klūd-. Cognates include Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌿𐍄𐍂𐍃 (hlūtrs), Welsh clir, and Latin cluō, clovāca.

2923.t: Uncertain. Compare Hittite 𒈠𒀀𒄴𒆷𒀸 (māḫlaš, “grapevine”), Hittite 𒊭𒈠𒇻 (šamalu-, “apple”), Hittite 𒊭𒄠𒇻 (šamlu-, “apple”) and Proto-Kartvelian *msxal- (“pear”).

2998.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥dḱomt, from *h₁néwn̥ (whence also ἐννέα (ennéa, “nine”)) + *déḱm̥t (whence also δέκα (déka, “ten”). Cognate with Latin nōnāgintā, Old Armenian իննսուն (innsun).

2973.t: According to Frisk an inherited Indo-European word for “throat, gorge”, cognate to Latin frūmen and Old Armenian երբուծ (erbuc), both from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg- (“to use, enjoy”), but phonetically this is somewhat problematic as the Greek form…

2943.t: From Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out”). Cognates include Albanian petë, Old English fæþm (English fathom), Latin pateō, patulus and pandō; and Avestan 𐬞𐬀𐬚𐬀𐬥𐬀 (paθana).

2991.t: From αἴρω (aírō, “to raise; to lift; to elevate”) + -σις (-sĭs).

2936.t: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ-er-os, from *bʰendʰ- (“to tie; bond, band”) and formally almost completely agreeing with Lithuanian beñdras (“common, shared”); compare also Sanskrit बन्धु (bandhu, “relative, kindred”).

2972.t: Perhaps from Proto-Hellenic *pā́uros, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w-, the irregular φ- (ph-) representing an expressive *pʰ-, as in Old Armenian փոքր (pʻokʻr, “small”).

2975.t: From χρίω (khríō, “to rub, smear”) + -μα (-ma). Later form of χρῖμα (khrîma) (LSJ).

2919.t: Possibly the same root as μήτηρ (mḗtēr).

2987.t: Uncertain. Could be related to σπάω (spắō, “to draw; to pull”).

2941.t: From περιβάλλω (peribállō) (from περι- (peri-) + βάλλω (bállō)) + -ος (-os). (garden): Compare typologically Proto-Iranian *paridayjah (the same PIE prefix) (whence παράδεισος (parádeisos)); English garden, Russian огоро́д (ogoród), Latin hortus.

2954.t: Of obscure origin. Furnée tentatively considers the word to be from Pre-Greek, based on a presumed connection to σοφός (sophós, “clever”), though Beekes is skeptical.

2913.t: Ablaut derivation from Proto-Indo-European *léymō (“lake”); compare λίμνη (límnē). See λειμών (leimṓn) for a descendant in a different ablaut grade.

2952.t: From πέκω (pékō, “to comb, to card; to shear”) + -ος (-os).

2956.t: From στάξ (stắx, “drop”) + -ών (-ṓn), of uncertain origin; also found in στάζω (stắzō, “to drop; to drip”).

2922.t: Beekes dismisses a derivation from ὤψ (ṓps, “face”) and prefers to derive it from Pre-Greek, comparing other words ending in "-ωψ", like κύνωψ (kúnōps) and κώνωψ (kṓnōps).

2925.t: According to Beekes, it may belong to νηρόν (nērón, “fresh water”) because of the characteristic property of this plant to follow the course of brooks.

2976.t: With ψάλιον (psálion, “curb-chain”) and ψαλόν (psalón, “bridle”) an Iranian borrowing.

2928.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *ksénwiyos. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀐𐀮𐀝𐀹𐀍 (ke-se-nu-wi-jo).

2988.t: Unknown, though of similar formation to ὁμαλός (homălós, “even, level”) and ἀταλός (atălós, “tender, shaking”). Possibly related to ἅπτω (hắptō, “to touch”).

2966.t: Perhaps from Proto-Hellenic *twáwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell, grow fat; become strong”). The immediate Proto-Indo-European formation is uncertain.

2909.t: Like many words ending in -υ (-ŭ), it is a loanword.
